attribution.note: Zitron is quoting his own earlier writing and re-endorses it in his own post. These are his words.

semantics.note: The proposition covers both parts: rising training costs and an ongoing, unavoidable cost. 'Not one-off R&D' reflects the surrounding framing that training is not mere R&D. It is a little stronger than the quoted sentence but is supported by the context.

contract.note: Using calendar 2025 against 2024 is a reasonable latest-completed-year reading. Separating training from inference and wider R&D is fair to the word 'training'. The contract rightly declines to read the claim as an accounting classification.

evidence.note: Shows OpenAI and Anthropic compute spend rose significantly from 2024 to 2025. It splits R&D from inference but does not isolate training, so it cannot settle the training-cost element.
OpenAI's disclosure documents a behavioural update to an existing model and the fixes that followed. This supports the recurring maintenance element only, with no cost data.
Covers 2024. Final training runs were about 10% of OpenAI's R&D compute. This warns against treating rising R&D compute as rising training or maintenance cost.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows total compute and R&D spend rising, and one documented maintenance update. No series isolates training or post-training spend from wider R&D. e3 suggests most R&D compute is not final training. The 'dramatically increasing training cost' part is therefore unverified, and the evidence does not show the full training budget is unavoidable.

attribution.note: The formula comes from The Information. Zitron restates and endorses it, and the 'easy to manipulate' judgement is his own.

semantics.note: Faithful. The proposition keeps both the formula (four weeks of API revenue x13) and the claim that product launches make it easy to manipulate. Filing it as an observation is defensible, though the manipulation part is a causal claim about susceptibility.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: launch-driven temporary spending can inflate the run rate. The contract rightly requires more than confirming the formula, and it does not demand proof of fraud.

evidence.note: The S-1, filed before the evaluation date, confirms a trailing 28-day x13 consumption formula and admits sensitivity to the measurement period. It does not show launch-driven temporary uplift or ease of manipulation in February to April 2026.

reviews.rationale: The formula is consistent with Anthropic's later S-1, which also admits short-window sensitivity. That is only the premise. No dated API revenue data separates temporary launch effects from sustained growth in the target period, so the core claim, that the figure is extremely easy to manipulate through launches, is neither supported nor contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The assertions sit inside a 'weird that people don't discuss' frame, but he plainly asserts them as facts.

semantics.note: Faithful to all three parts. The wording is hyperbolic, especially 'does not do anything that people discuss', but the parts are factual assertions about current state.

contract.note: Reading 'does not work' as lack of dependable completion, not total incapacity, is an ordinary and fair reading. Choosing Q1 2026 is reasonable for an undated present-tense claim. Assessing the three parts separately is appropriate.

evidence.note: Informal hands-on tests of Chrome Auto Browse in February 2026 found it needed nudging in almost every test. This loosely supports the AI-browser part for one product only, and says nothing about Operator.

Vendor benchmark from January 2026, published October 2026: 78% on hard browser tasks. It cuts against reading the claim as total incapacity, but it uses vendor-picked tasks, covers a different product, and says nothing about Operator.

reviews.rationale: No Q1 2026 evaluation of Operator is in the packet. One informal test of a single browser agent showed unreliability. A vendor benchmark showed substantial task completion. Neither is representative of AI browsers or of agent tasks generally, so none of the three parts is settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own emphatic assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition captures both the allegation of a lie and the factual claim that the entity was never formed. The $500B figure is kept as an identifier of the project.

contract.note: Treating legal formation as the concrete claim over January 2025 to April 2026 is fair. Requiring evidence of knowing falsity for 'lie' is fair, and construction alone is correctly held not to contradict the claim.

evidence.note: Oracle's CEO said in June 2025 that Stargate was 'still in formation'. This supports non-formation at that date only, not up to April 2026, and says nothing about intent.
OpenAI's July 2025 disclosure reports construction at Abilene and early workloads. This shows real activity under the Stargate name but does not address whether the joint-venture entity was formed.

reviews.rationale: The only formation evidence is a June 2025 remark that Stargate was still forming. No registry record or authoritative statement covers status through April 2026, and nothing shows the announcement was knowingly false. The construction evidence is real but does not decide the legal-entity question.
